articles.title: Like a rhinestone cowgirl – Dolly Parton’s most glorious, joyful and meta looks
articles.summary: Across six decades, the late country singer and pop culture icon turned self‑presentation into a flamboyant art form. • Don’t get Fashion Statement delivered to your inbox? Sign up here.
body: Dolly Parton may have had a record 25 US country No 1 singles, released 66 studio albums and earned six Golden Globe nominations, among many other achievements, but the Tennessee-born star also had an incredible number of fashion moments. “It costs a lot of money to look this cheap”, she famously quipped when asked about her style. As we bid her farewell, six Guardian writers reflect on their favourite Dolly looks.

While Parton wore a plethora of looks, sometimes up to 10 a day, you always knew what you were going to get. For over 60 years she held firm to her signature style – a silhouette that emphasised her tiny waist, along with high heels, higher hair and a heavy sprinkling of sparkle. In today’s world of image architects and constant reinvention, her continuity felt even more refreshing.
points: Across six decades, the late country singer and pop culture icon turned self‑presentation into a flamboyant art form. • Don’t get Fashion Statement delivered to your inbox?

articles.title: How do you define good health – and achieve it – in a broken US medical system?
articles.summary: In a new book, Dr Lucy McBride aims to help us navigate US healthcare – and tread carefully in the wellness industry. Most of us want to be healthy, but it’s easier said than done. In the US, people are caught between a broken medical system and a well-resourced wellness industry.
body: Over 25 years of practicing medicine, running a primary care practice in Washington DC, Dr Lucy McBride has seen patients struggle to navigate the medical system.

In her new book, Beyond the Prescription, McBride presents a practical framework for getting the best results from a flawed system. It begins with defining what health means to you. For one person, it might be running ultramarathons and extending longevity at any cost; for another, it might be balance and the freedom to indulge.

“The relationship between a patient and their primary care doctor is, at its best, one of the most protective forces in human health – and, right now, we’re systematically dismantling it,” says McBride over Zoom.

It’s no wonder patients feel unheard, unsatisfied and lost. We spoke about how people can advocate for themselves and pursue their vision of health. Our conversation has been condensed and edited for clarity.
points: In a new book, Dr Lucy McBride aims to help us navigate US healthcare – and tread carefully in the wellness industry.

articles.title: I don’t get along with my sister-in-law. Should I try to address the dynamic?
articles.summary: There are two things to consider, writes advice columnist Eleanor Gordon-Smith. Are you hurt by the way she treats you or the way she sees you? I’m struggling with a dynamic with my sister-in-law. We’re not a natural fit personality-wise, and I’ve tried to be mindful of that.
body: There’s a recurring pattern where she corrects me quite sharply, with an impatience that often feels disproportionate or plain mean. She might snap while I am talking to her parents (with whom I have a good relationship), laugh at how I pronounce a placename, or dismiss a question as though it’s too stupid to answer. These interactions are quick and barely noticeable to anyone else, although my daughter and husband have both observed and agreed it was pretty mean.
I’m unsure how to interpret this behaviour. More importantly, I don’t know what I owe – to myself, to her, and to the wider family in terms of responding.

Is this best addressed directly, even at the risk of creating awkwardness? At what point does tolerating this kind of interaction become a failure to stand up for myself? And might there be a cost in not trying to improve a relationship that could otherwise be supportive as we navigate the more ordinary trials of family life – ageing parents, illness and difficult decisions?
points: There are two things to consider, writes advice columnist Eleanor Gordon-Smith.
Are you hurt by the way she treats you or the way she sees you?

articles.title: No more crying over spills: I tested a robot vacuum that has a portable spot cleaner
articles.summary: Many robovacs can dust, mop and empty themselves at a dock, but the detachable cleaner sets the Eufy Omni E28 apart. 13 essentials we recommend for cleaning your home. Sign up for the Filter US newsletter, your weekly guide to buying fewer, better things.
body: There are a lot of robot vacuums to choose from these days. The Eufy Omni E28 may look like every other robot vacuum and mop, but it has one very big standout feature: its dock includes a detachable handheld carpet/fabric spot cleaner. Whenever you get a bad spill on the carpet, you’re supposed to be able to race over to the Omni dock, yank the “FlexiOne” portable deep cleaner’s handle to release it from the dock, plug it in where you need to deep clean, and eliminate that unsightly stain before it sets and leaves a permanent stain.

For a month, I used this robot vacuum to clean my home’s hardwood flooring, kitchen tiles and carpet. I also conducted a stain test to see how well its detachable deep cleaner could handle a variety of stains. I came away highly impressed with the cleaning power Eufy has packed into the E28, but you will also need to be a patient person who can handle a little noise.

articles.title: Actually, Dining Side-by-Side in Restaurants Is Good
articles.summary: All this week, the Eater Today newsletter is dedicated to editor Hot Takes, a way to release the pressure valve of crankiness that comes with sweating your way through the end of summer. This story was previously published as part of that series.
body: I love the unspoken rules around dining out; admittedly, even more so when they make me feel like I’m earning a gold star for good decorum. I like dressing up for the occasion; I like waiting obediently at the host stand ( See? I’m not pushy like other diners ); and I enjoy the martyrdom role of reorganizing the table’s contents as the meal unfolds (distributing food if we’re sharing small plates, consolidating finished plates, pouring carafes).

My adherence to a certain kind of behavior around the rituals of dining, however, goes out the window when it comes to seating. Specifically, when the option arises for one kind of seating arrangement that’s usually deemed corny: dining side by side.

articles.title: Why Is Loonen Water So Hyped?
articles.summary: After less than a year on the market, the bottled water is popping up everywhere.
body: To every generation, an expensive, hype-driven water is bestowed. Or at least, that’s what it’s felt like for the last quarter of a century. See: Fiji water, the status symbol bottle of the early 2000s, later replaced by millennial La Croix, itself usurped by the Gen Z cult of Liquid Death in the early 2020s.

In 2026, Loonen is part of a new vanguard of what’s being dubbed as “wellness waters,” bottled waters that appeal to people hoping to optimize their health. Some of these waters are infused with oxygen, others with hydrogen, and still others advertise that they’re alkaline and filled with electrolytes.

In an era where companies are built off what they infuse and add, Loonen does the opposite. The brand goes hard on what’s not in each bottle. Namely microplastics, the highly discussed health risk quickly becoming the scourge of the 2020s.

articles.title: This Fall, Leaf Peep from a Gondola, Helicopter, or Tree House
articles.summary: Go beyond the hike and try something a little different this year.
body: Americans call it “ leaf peeping,” while the Japanese call it “momijigari.” Whatever the culture, there’s a term for witnessing the changing colors of leaves, a universal act that spurs awe and wonder and makes one reflect on the passage of time. Fall foliage is worth booking a trip around, but you need not limit yourself to the standard hike or road trip. While we’ll always have these classic leaf-peeping excursions, there’s excitement in reinventing a ritual.

Once you start to experience the first chills of the season, consider getting a little whimsical: Mush your way through the Alaskan forest, float away on a hot air balloon in the Finger Lakes, or zipline past the Rockies. You could rent a run-of-the-mill cabin somewhere in the Hudson Valley, or you could go big with a tree house, complete with floor-to-ceiling windows. Ditch that standard New England inn and opt instead for a houseboat in coastal Maine, perfect for riverside scenery. The possibilities are endless, and the experiences on this list will ensure you see the changing colors of fall from all kinds of perspectives. Below, seven alternative ideas for leaf peeping across the US.

articles.title: Who Will Be the Next James Bond? 25 Possible Contenders
articles.summary: Here, Vogue charts the actors favored to be the next James Bond, from Callum Turner and Aaron Taylor-Johnson to Jack Barton and Dev Patel.
body: Then, a few months later, it emerged that Denis Villeneuve, the Oscar-nominated helmer of the Dune franchise, would be in the director’s chair. After that, we got some more intel, thanks to a report in Deadline. Per sources, Villeneuve “will embark on the search [for an actor] next year [2026] when he completes production on Dune: Part Three.” He’s apparently after “a fresh face,” ideally “an unknown,” possibly “in his late 20s or early 30s.”

So, who will it be? Jacob Elordi, as per DeuxMoi? Or, as originally reported, someone “from the British Isles,” like Callum Turner? It seems a final decision has yet to be made, and it could all still be up for grabs. To that end, browse all the current contenders for the role below.
